Soak means to make something completely and thoroughly wet by keeping it in liquid — or to become completely wet yourself. The key idea is not just wetness, but deep, total saturation over time. Think of a dry sponge dropped into a bucket of water. It doesn't just get wet on the surface — the water works its way all the way through it. That deep, thorough penetration is what "soak" is about.

1. To put something in liquid and leave it there

This is the most classic use. You place something into a liquid and let it sit — not for a second, but for a while — so the liquid can work its way deep inside it.

"Soak the beans in water overnight before cooking them."
"She soaked the stained shirt in soapy water for an hour."

The idea here is that time + liquid = deep penetration. You're not just rinsing something; you're letting the liquid do a slow, thorough job.

2. To make someone or something completely wet

When a liquid (especially rain) hits something hard and leaves it drenched all the way through — not just on the surface — that's soaking.

"The heavy rain soaked me completely. I had to change all my clothes."
"Don't leave the book outside. The rain will soak it."

Notice the sense of completeness here. You're not just a little wet — you're thoroughly wet.

3. To sit or bathe in liquid (used without an object)

When you yourself are the one sitting in liquid — relaxing in it — you use "soak" without an object. You are the thing being soaked.

"After a long day of hiking, she soaked in a hot bath for thirty minutes."
"He likes to soak in the hot tub every evening."

This is a very common and natural use. "Taking a long soak" means having a long, relaxing bath.

4. To penetrate through something (liquid moving through a material)

Sometimes liquid soaks through something — meaning it pushes its way from one side to the other.

"The ink soaked through the thin paper and stained the table beneath it."
"His shoes were so old that the water soaked straight through them."

Here, "soak through" describes liquid that doesn't stop at the surface — it travels all the way through the material.

5. To absorb liquid (often used with "up")

When a material pulls liquid into itself — like a sponge, a cloth, or soil — it soaks the liquid up.

"Use a paper towel to soak up the spilled juice."
"The dry earth soaked up every drop of rain within minutes."

The direction here is reversed from meaning #2. In meaning #2, liquid attacks something from the outside. Here, the thing draws the liquid into itself.

6. (Figurative) To absorb information, atmosphere, or experience deeply

This is one of the most important figurative uses. Just as a sponge absorbs water, a person can "absorb" an experience, knowledge, or atmosphere. When someone takes something in completely and enthusiastically, they soak it up or soak it in.

"She soaked up every word the professor said — she was fascinated by the topic."
"They arrived in Paris a day early just to soak in the atmosphere."
"Children soak up new languages much faster than adults."

This is used very naturally in everyday English. It carries a warm, positive connotation — a sense of being fully present and taking something in with joy or curiosity.

7. (Informal) To charge someone an unfairly high price

In informal English, if someone charges you way too much money — especially if they're taking advantage of you — they are said to have "soaked" you.

"That tourist restaurant really soaked us. $40 for a bowl of pasta!"
"The mechanic soaked him for repairs that cost twice what they should have."

This meaning is less common in everyday conversation but you will encounter it, especially in older writing or informal speech.

Phrasal verbs are combinations of a verb + a small word (like "up," "in," or "through") that together create a specific meaning. "Soak" has a few important ones.

Soak up — To absorb liquid, or figuratively to take in information, sunlight, praise, or atmosphere eagerly.

"The sponge soaked up the water instantly."
"She lay on the beach all day, soaking up the sun."
"He soaked up all the criticism and used it to improve."

Soak in — This has two uses. First, it means to sit immersed in liquid:

"She let her tired feet soak in warm water."

Second, it means to let something be fully understood or felt — often used when information or a reality needs time to settle in your mind:

"Take a moment to let that news soak in."
"He sat quietly, letting the beauty of the place soak in."

Soak through — For liquid to penetrate completely from one side to the other:

"The bandage soaked through within minutes — the cut was deep."

Understanding a word fully means knowing when not to use it. Here's how "soak" compares to words that seem similar:

Wet is just the general idea of being touched by water. A single drop of rain makes your sleeve wet. But it does not soak you. Soak implies far more thoroughness.

Drench means to make something completely wet, usually suddenly and all at once — like being hit by a wave or caught in a downpour. Drenching tends to be fast and violent. Soaking tends to be slower and deeper.

"A single wave drenched them from head to toe." (sudden, total)
"Sitting in the rain for an hour soaked their clothes." (gradual, thorough)

Steep is similar to soak but is almost always used for food or beverages — specifically when something is placed in hot liquid to release or take on flavor.

"Steep the tea for three minutes." (not "soak the tea")
"Steep the dried mushrooms in hot water to soften them."

You would not usually say "steep your feet" or "steep in a bath." That's where "soak" takes over.

Immerse means to put something completely under liquid. It describes the action of submerging, not the process of absorption. You can immerse something without soaking it (if you pull it out immediately), and you can soak something without fully immersing it (like soaking a cloth with water poured over it).
A Few Natural Collocations (Words Commonly Used with "Soak")

These are words and phrases you'll frequently see next to "soak" in real English:

  • soak overnight — soak the dried chickpeas overnight
  • soak in a bath / hot tub — I need to soak in a warm bath
  • soak up the sun — they spent the afternoon soaking up the sun
  • soak up the atmosphere — we walked around the city, soaking up the atmosphere
  • get soaked — we got completely soaked in the storm
  • soak through — the rain soaked through his jacket
  • let it soak in — pause and let that idea soak in

No matter which meaning you're looking at, there is always one underlying idea running through the word "soak": deep, thorough penetration or absorption — not quick, not shallow, but complete. Whether it's water moving into beans, rain soaking through a jacket, a person absorbing sunlight on a beach, or a student drinking in everything a teacher says — the word always carries that sense of going all the way in.
